intro.carita: Madhyama Carita (the middle episode), of which this is the battle chapter. In the recitation tradition the middle carita’s presiding form is Mahālakṣmī; this is the Gita Press viniyoga (printed before chapter 2), not a statement of the Purāṇa text. In the Gita Press pāṭha chapter 3 has no viniyoga of its own, only a dhyāna: the Goddess with the radiance of a thousand rising suns, in red silk, wearing a garland of heads, her breasts reddened, holding in her lotus hands a rosary, vidyā (usually understood as a book), the gesture of fearlessness and the boon, three-eyed, her crown bound with the moon, seated on a lotus.
intro.summary: Medhas goes on with the story (3.1). Seeing the army cut down, Mahiṣa’s general Cikṣura goes out to fight Ambikā and rains arrows on her like a cloud on Meru (3.2–3). She cuts his arrows to pieces as if at play, kills his horses and charioteer, breaks his bow and standard and pierces him (3.4–5); on foot with sword and shield he strikes the lion on the head and the Goddess on her arm, and the sword shatters (3.6–8). His flaming spear, hurled at Bhadrakālī, is broken by hers, and he dies with it (3.9–10). Cāmara comes on an elephant: his lance falls to her ‘hum’, his spear to her arrows (3.11–13), and the lion leaps onto the elephant, crashes to the ground with him and strikes off his head (3.14–16). The remaining generals fall in a catalogue — Udagra, Karāla, Uddhata, Bāṣkala, Tāmra, Andhaka, Ugrāsya, Ugravīrya, Mahāhanu, Biḍāla, Durdhara, Durmukha — each with the weapon that kills him (3.17–20). Mahiṣa himself, in his own buffalo shape, tramples the Goddess’s hosts with muzzle, hooves, tail, horns, speed, bellowing and breath (3.21–23), charges her lion (3.24), and in his rage breaks the earth, floods the ocean, tears the clouds and sends mountains crashing from the sky (3.25–27). Caṇḍikā turns her wrath to his death (3.28): she binds him with her noose; he sheds the buffalo and becomes a lion, then a man with a sword, then an elephant, each met by her weapons, and then the buffalo again, shaking the three worlds (3.29–33). She drinks and laughs, he flings mountains, and grinding them to dust she speaks (3.34–36): ‘Roar, fool, for a moment, while I drink; when I have slain you the gods will roar’ (3.37–38). She leaps on him, presses his neck with her foot and strikes him with her spear (3.39–40); caught half out of the buffalo’s mouth, still fighting, he is beheaded with her great sword (3.41–42). The asura army perishes, the gods rejoice and praise her, the Gandharvas sing and the Apsarases dance (3.43–44).
intro.forms: Ambikā, ‘the Mother’, the narrator’s commonest name for her (3.2, 3.12, 3.24, 3.30); Bhadrakālī, ‘the auspicious Kālī’ (3.9); Trinetrā, the three-eyed, and Parameśvarī, the Supreme Sovereign (3.19); Mahādevī (3.24); Caṇḍikā, ‘the fierce one’, from the turning point onward (3.28, 3.34, 3.35); and Jaganmātā, Mother of the world, in the moment of her fiercest act (3.34). Her final act — foot on the buffalo’s neck, spear and sword (3.40–42) — is the image painted and sculpted as Mahiṣāsuramardinī, a name the chapter itself does not use. Her lion and her hosts (gaṇas) fight as hers throughout (3.14–16, 3.21–24).
intro.significance: This is the battle the middle carita was building to: the Goddess made from the gods’ combined radiance in chapter 2 now does alone what the gods could not. The chapter moves outward in scale — a chariot duel, a wrestling match, a catalogue of deaths, then a buffalo whose rage reaches earth, ocean and sky (3.25–27) — and then inward to a single image: the asura caught halfway out of his own body (3.41). The gods take no part in the fighting; their part is joy and praise (3.43–44), which becomes the hymn of chapter 4 (4.2).
intro.grammar: A long run of reduplicated perfects as the narrative tense (ववर्ष, जघान, चिच्छेद, विव्याध, पफाल, जग्राह, चिक्षेप); periphrastic perfects of causatives (पातयामास, त्रासयामास, प्लावयामास, क्षोभयामास); passive narration with the agent in the instrumental (मृगारिणा … पृथक्कृतम्, 3.16; तया … देव्या … निपातितः, 3.42); locative absolutes (3.11, 3.21, 3.38); यावत् … तावत् with the present for an act about to happen (3.30); duals for the lion and Cāmara (3.15); a verse without a verb that waits for the next (3.22–23); and, in the Goddess’s one speech, the imperative and the future of the same root (गर्ज … गर्जिष्यन्ति, 3.38). Two verbs show the Purāṇic ātmanepada for the active (अमुञ्चत, 3.10; निरकृन्तत, 3.32).
intro.teaching: Literally, the chapter is a battle: generals die one by one, a buffalo-asura changes shape and is killed, and the gods celebrate. As teaching, the Śākta tradition reads the Goddess’s ease as the point — she cuts his arrows ‘as if at play’ (3.4), a sword breaks on her arm (3.8), a lance falls to a sound (3.12), and she drinks and laughs before the kill (3.34), so that the outcome is never in doubt (3.38). Modern readers often add a reflection of their own: an adversary that escapes by changing its shape (3.29–33) is overcome only when it is caught in the middle of the change (3.41–42), and the pride that roars (3.35, 3.38) is given its moment and no more. These readings are interpretations; the text itself states only the battle and the gods’ joy.
themes: The ease (līlā) of the Goddess in battle
The lion and the gaṇas: those who fight as hers
Mahiṣa’s rage at the scale of the world
Shape-changing and the escape that fails
Two intoxications: her drink and his pride
Victory turned into the gods’ praise

conclusion.narrative: Mahiṣa’s generals come out one at a time and die one at a time — Cikṣura in a chariot duel, Cāmara under the lion’s paw, the rest in a single catalogue. Then Mahiṣa himself fights as a buffalo, and his rage reaches earth, sea and sky. Caṇḍikā binds him; he slips from form to form — lion, man, elephant, buffalo again — until, with her foot on his neck, he is caught halfway out of the buffalo and beheaded. The chapter ends with what she promised in her one speech: the gods rejoicing, and the sound of praise (3.43–44), which chapter 4 takes up as a hymn.

constructions: The reduplicated perfect as the tense of narrative, singular and plural (जघान, चिच्छेद, विव्याध; ययुः, निपेतुः, तुष्टुवुः, ननृतुः).
The periphrastic perfect in -आमास for causatives and class-10 stems (पातयामास, त्रासयामास, चूर्णयामास, क्षोभयामास).
Passive narration: the past participle as verb, the agent in the instrumental (करप्रहारेण शिरश्चामरस्य पृथक्कृतम्, 3.16; देव्या … हतः, 3.17; तया … निपातितः, 3.42).
The locative absolute for the time of an action (हते तस्मिन् … चमूपतौ, 3.11; स्वसैन्ये संक्षीयमाणे, 3.21; मया त्वयि हते, 3.38).
यावत् … तावत् with the present for an act on the point of happening (3.30), and यावत् alone with the present for an act that runs alongside (3.38).
Distributive pronouns (कांश्चित् … अपरान् … अन्यान्) with instrumentals of means, gathered by one verb across two verses (3.22–23).
A chain of absolutives and a participle leading to one finite verb (उक्त्वा, समुत्पत्य, आरूढा, आक्रम्य … अताडयत्, 3.40).
The imperative and the future of one root set against each other (गर्ज गर्ज … गर्जिष्यन्ति, 3.38).
insights: Nothing the asuras bring reaches her: arrows are cut ‘as if at play’ (3.4), a sword shatters on her arm (3.8), a lance falls to a single sound (3.12).

The Goddess fights through what is hers: the lion kills Cāmara (3.14–16), the gaṇas born from her breath bear Mahiṣa’s first assault (3.21–23), and it is the attack on her lion that turns her anger on him (3.24, 3.32).

The asura’s disorder is cosmic, not private: earth, ocean, clouds and mountains suffer (3.25–27), and the three worlds tremble again when he resumes the buffalo (3.33) — which is why the one who acts is named Mother of the world (3.34).
Escape by changing form is answered form by form (3.29–33) and ends when he is caught between forms (3.41–42).
Her intoxication and his stand face to face: she drinks and laughs (3.34, 3.38), he is ‘drunk with pride’ (बलवीर्यमदोद्धतः, 3.35) and cannot see what he fights.
The victory belongs to the gods only as joy and praise (3.38, 3.43–44); the praise becomes the next chapter’s hymn (4.2).
conclusion.srividya: The chapter shares a few names and images with the Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa): Parameśvarī (3.19; name 396, परमेश्वरी), Caṇḍikā (3.28, 3.34, 3.35; name 755, चण्डिका), the red eyes of the drinking Goddess (3.34; compare name 432, मदघूर्णितरक्ताक्षी), her taste for madhu (3.38; compare name 510, मधुप्रीता), and the noose (3.29), which the Lalitā Sahasranāma gives its own meaning, attachment (name 8, रागस्वरूपपाशाढ्या). These are a shared Śākta vocabulary, not evidence that one text depends on the other. The battle with Mahiṣa belongs to the Devī Māhātmya alone, and no specifically Śrīvidyā doctrine is stated in this chapter.

key_verses.why: She cuts Cikṣura’s arrows to pieces ‘as if at play’ (लीलयैव) and kills his horses and charioteer.
Ambikā brings Cāmara’s lance to the ground, its fire gone, with the sound ‘hum’ alone.
She binds the great asura with her noose; caught, he sheds his buffalo form — the transformations begin.
Caṇḍikā, the Mother of the world, in fury drinks the supreme drink again and again and laughs, her eyes red.
‘Roar, fool, roar for a moment while I drink’ — the Goddess’s only speech: the gods will roar when he is slain.
Pinned by her foot, the asura is caught half-emerged from the buffalo’s mouth, held by her power.
Still half emerged and still fighting, he is struck down by the Goddess, who cuts off his head with her great sword.

sandhi_patterns: Visarga sandhi is the commonest junction: -aḥ → -o before voiced sounds (ततो देवी), -ḥ → s/ś before t/c (ततस्तौ, सेनानीश्चिक्षुरः), -ḥ → r before vowels and voiced sounds (बाणैर्यन्तारं), and the special rule for सः (स देवीं, 3.3; सच्छिन्नधन्वा, 3.6).
-aḥ before a vowel other than a loses its visarga and leaves the vowels apart (तत एवाशु, 3.31; अर्धनिष्क्रान्त एवासीद्, 3.41; अर्धनिष्क्रान्त एवासौ, 3.42).

Pūrvarūpa with avagraha (समरेऽसुरः, सोऽभून्महागजः), once on a dual verb that strict grammar would leave pragṛhya (युयुधातेऽतिसंरब्धौ, 3.15, kept as ārṣa); ā + ā written with the double avagraha (साऽऽरूढा, 3.40; पदाऽऽक्रान्तः, 3.41).

Consonant sandhi: t + ś → cch (तच्छूलं, 3.10), ch doubled after a short vowel (तस्यच्छित्त्वा, 3.4), t → n before nasals (तस्मान्नागान्महीं, 3.15), and n before c and ś (-आंश्च, -आञ्छृ-, 3.22, where the Gita Press spells out what the witnesses leave unapplied).
Optional visarga kept before a sibilant (मेरुगिरेः शृङ्गं, 3.3; ततः सिंहः, 3.14); savarṇa-dīrgha, guṇa and vṛddhi across words and inside compounds (लीलयैव, शरोत्करान्).
samasa: Bahuvrīhis of loss in a row (छिन्नधन्वा, विरथः, हताश्वः, हतसारथिः, 3.5–6), with धनुस् replaced by धन्वन् at the end of a bahuvrīhi.
Bahuvrīhis as epithets and names (त्रिनेत्रा, अरुणलोचना, खड्गपाणिः; the generals उग्रास्य, उग्रवीर्य, महाहनु, दुर्मुख).
Upapada tatpuruṣas with verbal roots (सेनानीः, तोयदः, तुरगान्, आशुगैः, त्रिदशार्दनः, भूधरान्).
Nested tṛtīyā tatpuruṣas of cause in the cosmic verses (वेगभ्रमणविक्षुण्णा, धुतशृङ्गविभिन्नाः, श्वासानिलास्ताः, 3.26–27).
Dvandvas: samāhāra खड्गचर्मणा (3.31, neuter singular), itaretara दन्तमुष्टितलैः (3.17), and a dvandva inside सचराचरम् (3.33).
Karmadhārayas with महा- (महासुरः, महामृधे, महागजः, महासिना), and the long adverbial bahuvrīhi मदोद्धूतमुखरागाकुलाक्षरम् (3.36).
grammar_notes: Purāṇic ātmanepada for the active: अमुञ्चत (3.10) and निरकृन्तत (3.32), the latter from a parasmaipada root; neither is a passive.
The genitive marks the target of a throw where the locative would be stricter: देव्याः with मुमोच (3.12), तस्य with पाशं क्षिप्त्वा (3.29).
Verbs carried across lines and verses: the second line of 3.18 is governed by जघान in 3.19; 3.22 waits for पातयामास in 3.23; स च महासुरः (3.10) supplies नीतः from नीतम्.
The same participle is printed युद्ध्यमानौ (3.15) and युध्यमानः (3.42); the doubled stop is the Gita Press’s spelling, not another form.
Active past participles of motion and posture taking objects: तं महासुरम् आरूढा (3.40), माहिषं वपुः आस्थितः (3.33).
themes: Līlā: the ease of the Goddess
The lion and the gaṇas as hers
uncertain: 3.15: युद्ध्यमानौ (Gita Press) / युध्यमानौ (GRETIL, Freund) — orthographic; the same form.
3.22: चान्याञ्छृङ्गाभ्यां (Gita Press) / चान्यान्शृङ्गाभ्यां (GRETIL, Freund) — orthographic; the sandhi spelled out or left unapplied.

Interpretive doubts, none about the reading, are flagged on 3.12 (देव्याः as target of मुमोच or with हुंकाराभिहताम्), 3.36 (whether the flushed face is the Goddess’s or the asura’s) and 3.41 (देव्याः or देव्या with वीर्येण).
The Purāṇa recension in GRETIL’s Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa carries further verses in 3.21 and 3.43 that the Gita Press Saptaśatī does not; nothing was added (corrections.json, recension notes).

mantras.lit: Having seen that army being slaughtered, the great asura, the general Cikṣura, in anger then went to fight Ambikā.
mantras.tr: Seeing his army cut down, the mighty asura Cikṣura, Mahiṣa’s general, went in fury to fight Ambikā.
mantras.tr_note: ‘His army’ and ‘Mahiṣa’s general’ make explicit what तत् and सेनानीः imply (Cikṣura is named Mahiṣa’s general at 2.40).

comm.t: The general steps forward when the army falls. Cikṣura was named first among Mahiṣa’s commanders at 2.40; now he faces the Goddess alone.

In the Gita Press pāṭha, chapters 2–4 form the middle carita, whose presiding form is Mahālakṣmī (a liturgical attribution). Chapter 3 is its battle: the generals fall one by one (3.2–20) before Mahiṣa himself comes forward (3.21).

mantras.tr: In the battle the asura poured a storm of arrows on the Goddess, as a cloud pours its rain on the summit of Meru.

comm.t: The simile says what the arrows achieve: as much as rain does to Meru. The mountain is wetted, not moved.
A modern reading: the image places the attack and its target on different scales. What rains on the Goddess is weather; she is the mountain.

mantras.anvaya_en: Absolutive clause (शरोत्करान् छित्त्वा) followed by the main verb जघान with two objects (तुरगान्, यन्तारम्).
mantras.lit: Then the Goddess, having cut his masses of arrows merely in play, struck down with arrows the horses and also the driver of the horses.
mantras.tr: The Goddess cut his arrows to pieces as if at play, and with her own arrows she killed his horses and their charioteer.

comm.t: The first answer is defensive, then she disables the chariot: horses and driver. लीलया एव — ‘just in play’ — repeats the phrase used of her at 2.50 (लीलयैव प्रचिच्छेद).
The ease of the Goddess (लीला) runs through the battle books: the same words recur at 8.31 and 10.13. The battle costs her nothing; the effort is all on the asuras’ side.

mantras.anvaya_en: Subject (देवी) continued from 3.4; two coordinated verbs, चिच्छेद with two objects and विव्याध with one object, a locative of place and an instrument.
mantras.lit: And she at once cut (his) bow and the very lofty banner; and she also pierced in the limbs with swift-going (arrows) him whose bow was cut.
mantras.tr: At once she cut through his bow and his towering standard, and with swift arrows she pierced the disarmed asura all over his body.

comm.t: The chariot duel runs its course: horses and driver (3.4), bow and standard, then the warrior himself. The sequence follows the conventions of epic chariot combat.
The banner (ध्वज) is the warrior’s emblem; to cut it down is to announce his defeat before he falls.

samasa.alt: The first member could also be an itaretara dvandva (खड्गचर्मणी, ‘sword and shield’); 3.31 has the singular खड्गचर्मणा, which supports the samāhāra reading.

mantras.anvaya: छिन्नधन्वा विरथः हताश्वः हतसारथिः खड्गचर्मधरः सः असुरः तां देवीम् अभ्यधावत।
mantras.anvaya_en: One subject (सः … असुरः) carrying five predicate adjectives — four bahuvrīhis of loss and one of arms — and the verb अभ्यधावत with its object.
mantras.lit: He, with bow cut, chariotless, horses slain, charioteer slain, rushed at that Goddess, the asura holding sword and shield.
mantras.tr: Bow broken, chariot gone, horses and charioteer slain, the asura took up sword and shield and charged at the Goddess.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Took up’ renders the compound खड्गचर्मधरः ‘bearing sword and shield’ as an action.

comm.t: The line of four bahuvrīhis sums up 3.4–5: everything a chariot-warrior fights with is gone. Cikṣura goes on, on foot.
The Purāṇa honours the courage of the asura generals even as they fall; none of them flees.

mantras.anvaya_en: Absolutive clause with its own locative of the part (सिंहं मूर्धनि आहत्य), then the main clause on the same pattern (देवीं सव्ये भुजे आजघान).
mantras.lit: Having struck the lion on the head with his sharp-edged sword, he, very swift, struck the Goddess too on the left arm.
mantras.tr: Moving with great speed, he struck the lion on the head with his keen-edged sword, and then struck the Goddess herself on her left arm.

comm.t: Cikṣura attacks both the mount and its rider. The lion is the Goddess’s vāhana, given to her by Himavat (2.29), and a fighter in its own right (2.51–52, 3.14–16).

mantras.anvaya: (हे) नृपनन्दन, खड्गः तस्याः भुजं प्राप्य पफाल। ततः कोपात् अरुणलोचनः सः शूलं जग्राह।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two sentences: the sword as subject of an absolutive and of पफाल; then Cikṣura as subject of जग्राह. The vocative interrupts the narrative.
mantras.lit: Reaching her arm, the sword shattered, O son of a king. Then he, red-eyed with anger, seized a spear.
mantras.tr: The sword shattered as it met her arm, O prince. Then, his eyes red with rage, he seized a spear.

comm.t: The sword breaks on the Goddess’s arm — she is not wounded. Medhas’s vocative नृपनन्दन recalls the frame: the battle is a story told to King Suratha.
Weapons breaking against the Goddess is a recurring sign in the battle books that no created weapon reaches her.

mantras.lit: And then the great asura hurled it, blazing fiercely with radiance like the sun’s disc from the sky, at Bhadrakālī.
mantras.tr: Then the great asura hurled the spear at Bhadrakālī, flaming with light like the sun’s disc falling from the sky.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Falling’ is supplied to complete the simile with अम्बरात् ‘from the sky’.

comm.t: The spear is thrown, blazing like the sun. Here the narrator names the Goddess Bhadrakālī, the ‘auspicious Kālī’; the name returns at 4.39, when she vanishes after granting the gods’ boon.

mantras.anvaya_en: First sentence: absolutive and main verb. Second: a passive participle as verb, with an elliptical second subject whose participle is supplied.
mantras.lit: Seeing that spear flying at (her), the Goddess hurled a spear. By it that spear was brought to a hundred pieces, and (so was) the great asura.
mantras.tr: Seeing the spear flying at her, the Goddess hurled her own. It shattered his spear into a hundred pieces — and the great asura with it.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Her own’ and ‘his’ distinguish the two spears; ‘with it’ renders the elliptical स च महासुरः.

comm.t: Cikṣura’s death is told in three words, स च महासुरः, with the verb left to be supplied. 3.11 confirms it: हते तस्मिन् ‘when he was slain’.
The Goddess answers each weapon with its like — arrow with arrow, spear with spear — and hers prevails.

mantras.lit: That mighty commander of Mahiṣa having been slain, Cāmara, tormentor of the gods, came, mounted on an elephant.
mantras.tr: When Mahiṣa’s mighty general had fallen, Cāmara, the scourge of the gods, came forward on an elephant.

comm.t: The second general. Cāmara was named among the commanders at 2.41 (युयुधे चामरः); his epithet त्रिदशार्दनः was used of the whole asura host at 2.60.

morph.note: Perfect of √मुच्: reduplication मु- and guṇa u → o (मु-मोच).

The genitive marks the person aimed at, where 3.9 used the locative (भद्रकाल्याम्); a usage found in epic narrative.

mantras.anvaya: अथ सः अपि देव्याः शक्तिं मुमोच। अम्बिका तां (शक्तिं) द्रुतं हुंकाराभिहतां निष्प्रभां भूमौ पातयामास।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two sentences. In the second, ताम् carries two predicative adjectives (हुंकाराभिहताम्, निष्प्रभाम्): she brought it down, struck by her ‘hum’ and dulled.
mantras.lit: He too then released a lance at the Goddess. Ambikā swiftly made it, struck by (her) ‘hum’ (and) lustreless, fall to the ground.
mantras.tr: He in turn hurled a lance at the Goddess; but Ambikā, with a single cry of ‘hum’, struck it down at once, and it fell to the ground, its fire gone out.
mantras.tr_note: ‘A single cry’ renders हुंकार ‘the sound hum’; the lit. translation keeps the compound’s order.

comm.t: Here no weapon is needed: the Goddess’s ‘hum’ alone brings the lance down. देव्याः is best taken as the target of मुमोच (‘at the Goddess’).
The hūṃkāra recurs as the Goddess’s weapon: at 6.13 it burns Dhūmralocana to ash (हुंकारेणैव तं भस्म), and at 10.13 it breaks Śumbha’s divine missiles.

flags.uncertain: देव्याः could also be construed with हुंकाराभिहताम् (‘struck by the Goddess’s hum’), a genitive qualifying the first member of a compound; the analysis prefers the target sense with मुमोच.

mantras.anvaya: शक्तिं भग्नां निपतितां दृष्ट्वा क्रोधसमन्वितः चामरः शूलं चिक्षेप। सा तत् अपि बाणैः अच्छिनत्।
mantras.anvaya_en: First sentence: absolutive clause with a double predicate (भग्नाम्, निपतिताम्), then the main verb. Second: a new subject (सा) and verb.
mantras.lit: Seeing the lance broken and fallen, Cāmara, filled with fury, hurled a spear. She cut that too with arrows.
mantras.tr: Seeing his lance broken on the ground, Cāmara, beside himself with rage, flung a spear; and that too she cut down with her arrows.

comm.t: Cāmara repeats Cikṣura’s sequence (lance, then spear), with the same result. The short clause बाणैस्तदपि साच्छिनत् dismisses it in half a line.

mantras.anvaya: ततः सिंहः समुत्पत्य गजकुम्भान्तरे स्थितः (सन्) तेन त्रिदशारिणा (सह) बाहुयुद्धेन उच्चैः युयुधे।
mantras.anvaya_en: Absolutive and participle describe the lion’s leap and position; the main verb युयुधे takes the opponent in the instrumental.
mantras.lit: Then the lion, having leapt up, standing between the elephant’s frontal globes, fought fiercely in arm-to-arm combat with him, the enemy of the gods.
mantras.tr: Then the lion sprang up onto the elephant’s brow and, planted there, grappled fiercely with that enemy of the gods.

comm.t: The lion takes over the fight with Cāmara on his own elephant. ‘Arm-fighting’ (बाहुयुद्ध) is the term for wrestling, used here of a lion against an asura.

sandhi.note: The text joins -e + a- → -e’- (avagraha). Strictly, a dual form ending in -e — verbal as well as nominal — is pragṛhya and should stand unjoined (युयुधाते अतिसंरब्धौ). The printed pūrvarūpa is a laxity of epic and Purāṇic verse (ārṣa); the text is kept as it stands.

morph.note: Present participle of the divādi stem युध्य- with -मान, dual. The Gita Press spells it with the stop doubled before its aspirate (युद्ध्य-); GRETIL and Freund read युध्यमानौ. It is the same form — an orthographic variant (corrections.json).
Perfect ātmanepada, 3rd dual: reduplicated युयुध्- with -आते. Compare युयुधे (3rd sg.) in 3.14.
With a verb of motion the kta participle is active and serves as the finite verb: ‘the two went (down)’.

mantras.anvaya: ततः तु युद्ध्यमानौ तौ तस्मात् नागात् महीं गतौ। अतिसंरब्धौ (तौ) अतिदारुणैः प्रहारैः युयुधाते।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two sentences with the same dual subject: a participle of motion as verb, then the perfect युयुधाते with an instrumental of means.
mantras.lit: Then the two, fighting, went from that elephant to the ground. Wild with fury, they fought with most terrible blows.
mantras.tr: Locked in combat, the two crashed from the elephant to the ground, and there, in towering rage, fought on with savage blows.

comm.t: Lion and asura fall together from the elephant and continue on the ground. The dual forms (युद्ध्यमानौ, तौ, गतौ, युयुधाते, अतिसंरब्धौ) keep the pair in view through the whole verse.

Passive construction: the head is the subject (शिरः, neuter, hence कृतम्) and the lion the agent in the instrumental (मृगारिणा). पृथक् कृ ‘to make separate, sever’.

mantras.anvaya: ततः मृगारिणा वेगात् खम् उत्पत्य निपत्य च करप्रहारेण चामरस्य शिरः पृथक् कृतम्।
mantras.anvaya_en: A passive sentence: agent (मृगारिणा) with two absolutives, instrument (करप्रहारेण), subject (शिरः) and the participle कृतम् as verb.
mantras.lit: Then, by the enemy of beasts, having leapt with speed into the sky and come down, with a blow of the paw, the head of Cāmara was made separate.
mantras.tr: Then the lion sprang swiftly into the air and, coming down, struck off Cāmara’s head with a blow of its paw.
mantras.tr_note: The Sanskrit is passive (‘Cāmara’s head was severed by the lion’); the translation makes it active.

comm.t: The lion, not the Goddess, kills Cāmara. Her mount fights as her ally, as it did at 2.51–52, where it ranged through the asura army like fire through a forest.

morph.note: Past participle of the causative (नि + पातय- + त): ‘made to fall’, i.e. struck down. Contrast निपतिता ‘fallen’ (3.13), from the simple verb.
Passive participle as the verb, with the agent in the instrumental (देव्या). The agent of निपातितः in the second line is not restated; the nearest is देव्या.

mantras.anvaya: रणे देव्या शिलावृक्षादिभिः उदग्रः च हतः, दन्तमुष्टितलैः च एव करालः च निपातितः।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two passive clauses on one pattern: instrument + subject + participle. देव्या, stated in the first, is understood in the second.
mantras.lit: And Udagra was slain in battle by the Goddess with rocks, trees and the like; and Karāla too was struck down with teeth, fists and palms.
mantras.tr: Udagra was slain in battle by the Goddess with boulders, trees and the like; and Karāla was felled with teeth, fists and blows of the open hand.

comm.t: Two more generals fall. Udagra was named at 2.41 (उदग्राख्यो महासुरः). The weapons are those of close, improvised combat — rocks, trees, teeth, fists — unlike the arrows and spears so far.

The text names only देव्या as agent. Rocks, trees and teeth are also the weapons of her lion and of the gaṇas born from her breath (2.52–53), who fight as extensions of her; the Sanskrit itself does not say whose hands they were.

mantras.anvaya: क्रुद्धा देवी गदापातैः उद्धतं च चूर्णयामास, भिन्दिपालेन वाष्कलं, बाणैः ताम्रं तथा अन्धकं (जघान)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line is complete. The second lists three more accusatives, each with its weapon; their verb is not stated, and जघान in 3.19 (or चूर्णयामास, extended) governs them.
mantras.lit: The Goddess, enraged, crushed Uddhata with blows of the mace; Bāṣkala with a bhindipāla, Tāmra and likewise Andhaka with arrows.
mantras.tr: In her fury the Goddess crushed Uddhata with her mace; Bāṣkala she struck down with a javelin, and Tāmra and Andhaka with her arrows.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Struck down’ is supplied for the second line, which has no verb of its own.

comm.t: A catalogue of deaths: each general is named with the weapon that kills him. The bhindipāla is among the weapons of the asuras at 2.47 and of the gaṇas at 2.53.

Of the names, Bāṣkala appears among the commanders at 2.43; Uddhata, Tāmra and Andhaka are named here for the first time. उद्धतम् could be taken as an adjective (‘the arrogant one’), but the list of names around it favours a proper name.

mantras.lit: And the three-eyed Supreme Sovereign slew with the trident Ugrāsya and Ugravīrya, and likewise Mahāhanu.
mantras.tr: And with her trident the three-eyed Supreme Goddess slew Ugrāsya, Ugravīrya and Mahāhanu.

comm.t: Three more generals fall to the trident. The narrator varies her names through the battle — Ambikā (3.2, 3.12), Bhadrakālī (3.9), Devī — and here Trinetrā, ‘the three-eyed’, and Parameśvarī, ‘Supreme Sovereign’, the title Brahmā gave her in his hymn (1.82).
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the same title as name 396, परमेश्वरी. The shared name reflects a common Śākta vocabulary; the two texts are separate works.

mantras.anvaya: (देवी) असिना बिडालस्य शिरः कायात् वै पातयामास। दुर्धरं दुर्मुखं च उभौ शरैः यमक्षयं निन्ये।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two sentences with the Goddess as understood subject: object with its genitive and an ablative of separation; then two objects summed up by उभौ, an instrument and a goal.
mantras.lit: With the sword she indeed made Biḍāla’s head fall from his body; Durdhara and Durmukha, both, she led with arrows to the abode of Yama.
mantras.tr: With her sword she struck Biḍāla’s head from his body, and with her arrows she sent both Durdhara and Durmukha to the house of Death.

comm.t: The catalogue ends. Biḍāla was named among the commanders at 2.44 (बिडालाख्यः); Durdhara and Durmukha appear here for the first time. With them the named generals are all dead, and Mahiṣa must come himself (3.21).

samasa.alt: Also analysed as a madhyamapadalopī compound, महिषरूपः असुरः ‘the asura in buffalo form’; the karmadhāraya is simpler and fits the verse, which names his buffalo form separately.

mantras.anvaya: एवं स्वसैन्ये संक्षीयमाणे तु महिषासुरः माहिषेण स्वरूपेण तान् गणान् त्रासयामास।
mantras.anvaya_en: A locative absolute (स्वसैन्ये संक्षीयमाणे) sets the time; the main clause has subject, instrumental of manner, object and the causative perfect.
mantras.lit: As his own army was thus being destroyed, Mahiṣāsura, in his own buffalo form, terrified those hosts.
mantras.tr: As his army wasted away, Mahiṣāsura himself, in his own buffalo shape, fell upon the Goddess’s hosts and struck terror into them.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Fell upon’ anticipates 3.22–23; ‘the Goddess’s hosts’ makes explicit who तान् गणान् are.

comm.t: Mahiṣa himself enters the battle. The gaṇas he terrifies are the hosts born from the Goddess’s breaths (2.52–53).

The phrase माहिषेण स्वरूपेण ‘in his own buffalo form’ marks the buffalo as Mahiṣa’s native shape. The other forms he takes later — lion, man with a sword, elephant (3.30–32) — are assumed, and at 3.33 he takes the buffalo body again.

samasa.literal: by a blow of the snout

morph.note: The indefinite pronoun declines in its first part (कश्चित्, कांश्चित्, केचित्): accusative plural ‘some’. कांश्चित् … अपरान् … अन्यान् distribute the victims: ‘some … others … others’.
Past participle of the causative दारय- (वि + √दॄ): ‘made to burst, ripped open’.
Instrumental dual: the buffalo’s pair of horns.

mantras.anvaya: कांश्चित् तुण्डप्रहारेण, तथा अपरान् खुरक्षेपैः, अन्यान् च लाङ्गूलताडितान्, (अन्यान्) च शृङ्गाभ्यां विदारितान् (पातयामास, 3.23)।
mantras.anvaya_en: A verse without a verb: four groups of victims in the accusative, each with how Mahiṣa struck them. The verb पातयामास comes in 3.23.
mantras.lit: Some with blows of his muzzle, likewise others with kicks of his hooves, and others lashed by his tail, and (others) torn open with his two horns —
mantras.tr: Some he struck down with blows of his muzzle, others with his hooves; others he lashed with his tail, and others he ripped open with his horns —
mantras.tr_note: The verse continues into 3.23, whose verb पातयामास (‘he felled’) is anticipated here as ‘struck down’.

comm.t: Mahiṣa fights as a buffalo, with every part of the animal: muzzle, hooves, tail, horns. The sentence runs on into 3.23, where the verb (‘he felled them on the ground’) finally comes.

samasa.alt: Also possible as a karmadhāraya, निःश्वासः एव पवनः ‘the breath which is a wind’; the sense is the same. निःश्वास is itself a prefixed noun (निस् + √श्वस् + घञ्), not a compound.

morph.note: Periphrastic perfect of the causative: पातय- + आम् + the perfect of √अस् (आस). Causatives and other derived stems form their perfect this way. ‘Made to fall’ = ‘felled’.

Action noun in -अन (ल्युट्) from √भ्रम् ‘to wander, whirl’; neuter.

mantras.anvaya: (महिषासुरः) कांश्चित् वेगेन, अपरान् नादेन भ्रमणेन च, अन्यान् निःश्वासपवनेन भूतले पातयामास।
mantras.anvaya_en: पातयामास is the verb for the whole list begun in 3.22: the accusatives there (कांश्चित्, अपरान्, अन्यान्, the participles ताडितान्, विदारितान्) and here all depend on it, each with its own instrumental of means.
mantras.lit: Some by (his) charge, others by (his) bellowing and whirling, and others by the wind of (his) breath, he felled on the ground.
mantras.tr: Some he threw to the ground by the force of his charge, others with his bellowing and his wheeling about, and others again with the blast of his breath.
mantras.tr_note: The verb completes the sentence begun in 3.22; the subject, Mahiṣāsura, is named in 3.21.

comm.t: The buffalo’s rampage through the Goddess’s gaṇas ends: every part of the animal — speed, voice, motion, breath — is a weapon. The single verb पातयामास gathers the long list of 3.22–23.

The gaṇas he fells were born from the Goddess’s own breath in battle (निःश्वासान् मुमुचे … त एव सद्यः सम्भूता गणाः, 2.52–53). Here the buffalo fells them with the wind of his breath: breath against breath, before the duel itself begins.

mantras.anvaya_en: Two sentences: the asura’s charge (absolutive, object, infinitive of purpose, verb) and the Goddess’s answer (कोपं चक्रे).
mantras.lit: Having struck down the army of the Pramathas, that asura rushed forward to kill the great Goddess’s lion. Then Ambikā became angry.
mantras.tr: Having cut down the Goddess’s host, the demon charged to kill the great Goddess’s lion. At that, Ambikā grew angry.

comm.t: With the gaṇas down, Mahiṣa goes for the lion, the Goddess’s mount (given her by Himavān, 2.29). The attack on her vāhana is what turns her anger on him; from here the duel is between the two of them.
प्रमथ ‘tormentor’ is a name used elsewhere for Śiva’s troops; here it names the gaṇas the Goddess produced from her breath (2.53).

mantras.anvaya_en: One subject with two epithets; two finite verbs joined by च … च.
mantras.lit: He too, of great might, out of anger, crushing the surface of the earth with (his) hooves, both hurled lofty mountains with (his) two horns and bellowed.
mantras.tr: He too, in his fury, mighty, churning the earth with his hooves, tossed high mountains with his horns and bellowed.

comm.t: Anger answers anger: the Goddess’s कोप (3.24) is met by his (कोपात्). The buffalo’s violence now reaches the scale of the world — earth, mountains, and in the next verses the ocean and the clouds. Verses 3.25–27 strike each region in turn: earth, water, then the sky.

mantras.anvaya: तस्य वेगभ्रमणविक्षुण्णा मही व्यशीर्यत। लाङ्गूलेन आहतः अब्धिः च सर्वतः प्लावयामास।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two clauses, earth and ocean. तस्य depends on the idea of ‘rush and whirling’ inside the compound (a genitive construed with a compound member, accepted in epic usage).
mantras.lit: The earth, crushed by his rush and whirling, split apart; and the ocean, lashed by (his) tail, flooded on every side.
mantras.tr: Pounded by his charging and wheeling, the earth broke apart; and the ocean, lashed by his tail, overflowed on every side.

comm.t: Earth and water suffer next: the ground splits under his hooves and turning, the sea spills over its shores at a blow of his tail.
A modern reading: the buffalo’s rage does not stay inside the battle. Unchecked force damages the ground everyone stands on — which is why, in this story, it has to be stopped.

mantras.anvaya_en: Two clauses, clouds and mountains, each subject carrying a compound participle of cause.
mantras.lit: And the clouds, split by (his) tossing horns, went piece by piece; mountains thrown by the wind of (his) breath fell by the hundred from the sky.
mantras.tr: The clouds, torn by his tossing horns, were shredded to pieces, and mountains flung up by the blast of his breath came crashing down from the sky by the hundred.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Flung up’ makes explicit what अस्ताः ‘thrown’ implies, since they fall ‘from the sky’.

comm.t: The sky is struck last: the clouds are torn and mountains rain down. The picture completes the cosmic scale of 3.25–27, after which the narrator turns to the Goddess (3.28). अचल, ‘the immovable’, is a common word for a mountain; the paradox is deliberate — what cannot move is thrown about by his breath.

mantras.lit: Seeing the great asura thus swollen with rage and rushing upon (her), Caṇḍikā then made (her) anger for his slaying.
mantras.tr: Seeing the great demon bearing down on her, bursting with rage, Caṇḍikā then turned her wrath to his destruction.
mantras.tr_note: कोपम् अकरोत् ‘made anger’ is rendered ‘turned her wrath’; तद्वधाय gives its aim.

comm.t: A turning point. Her anger in 3.24 was at the attack on her lion; now it is directed (तद्वधाय) at his death. From 3.29 on she acts against Mahiṣa alone.

Caṇḍikā, the name the narrator uses here and in 3.34–35, is also a name of the Goddess in the Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa), name 755, चण्डिका. The two texts share the name; the battle here belongs to the Devī Māhātmya alone.

The genitive marks the person towards whom the noose is thrown; a locative or dative would be the stricter construction. It cannot mean ‘his noose’: the noose is the Goddess’s, the gift of the lord of waters (पाशं चाम्बुपतिर्ददौ, 2.23).

mantras.anvaya: सा तस्य (उपरि) पाशं क्षिप्त्वा वै तं महासुरं बबन्ध। महामृधे बद्धः सः अपि माहिषं रूपं तत्याज।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two sentences: the binding (absolutive + perfect) and his response, with बद्धः as a participle of circumstance.
mantras.lit: She, having cast the noose upon him, indeed bound that great asura. He too, bound in the great battle, gave up (his) buffalo form.
mantras.tr: She cast her noose over him and bound the great demon. Caught fast in the great battle, he shed his buffalo form.

comm.t: The noose — Varuṇa’s gift (2.23) — holds the buffalo, and the asura escapes it by escaping his body: the shape-changing of 3.29–33 begins. Each new form is a way out of what has caught the last one.
A modern reading: what is bound in one form slips away into another. The pursuit through lion, man and elephant shows a problem that keeps changing its shape until it is met at its root.

mantras.lit: Then at once he became a lion. Just as Ambikā is cutting off his head, at that moment a man, sword in hand, was seen.
mantras.tr: At once he became a lion. But just as Ambikā was about to cut off its head, a man appeared, sword in hand.
mantras.tr_note: The Sanskrit present after यावत् is rendered by the English past of intention (‘was about to’).

comm.t: Two changes in one verse: buffalo to lion, lion to armed man. The यावत् … तावत् construction makes the escape exact — the new form appears at the very instant of the blow.

mantras.anvaya: ततः एव आशु देवी तं पुरुषं खड्गचर्मणा सार्धं सायकैः चिच्छेद। ततः सः महागजः अभूत्।
mantras.anvaya_en: पुरुषम् and तम् refer to the same man: the second line resumes him with the pronoun so that ‘with his sword and shield’ can be added.
mantras.lit: Right then the Goddess swiftly cut down the man with arrows — him together with (his) sword and shield. Then he became a great elephant.
mantras.tr: At that very moment the Goddess cut the man down with her arrows, sword, shield and all. Then he turned into a huge elephant.

comm.t: The man is cut down with the very arms he appeared with (3.30), and the asura escapes again, now as an elephant: buffalo, lion, man, elephant.

mantras.lit: And with (his) trunk he dragged that great lion and trumpeted. But the Goddess cut off with (her) sword the trunk of (him) dragging.
mantras.tr: With his trunk he dragged at the great lion, trumpeting; but as he dragged, the Goddess cut off his trunk with her sword.

comm.t: As in 3.24, the asura goes for the lion, and again the Goddess answers for it. The elephant’s weapon, its trunk, is cut off in the act of using it.

mantras.tr: Then the great demon took on his buffalo body once more and, as before, threw the three worlds into turmoil, all that moves and all that stands still.

comm.t: After lion, man and elephant the asura returns to the buffalo, and the cosmic disorder of 3.25–27 begins again (तथैव ‘just as before’). The circle of transformations is closed; the next move is the Goddess’s.

mantras.lit: Then the enraged Mother of the world, Caṇḍikā, drank the supreme drink again and again, and indeed laughed, red-eyed.
mantras.tr: Then Caṇḍikā, the Mother of the world, in her fury drank the supreme drink again and again, and laughed, her eyes red.

comm.t: The Goddess drinks and laughs in the face of the asura’s renewed onslaught. The drink is called only ‘the supreme drink’ here; she herself calls it मधु in 3.38. The drinking-vessel is one of her gifts in chapter 2: Kubera gave her a cup never empty of wine (ददावशून्यं सुरया पानपात्रं धनाधिपः, 2.30).
The Goddess’s drinking and laughter before the kill are read in the Śākta tradition as signs of her fierce form and of her ease: the battle is play to her (cf. लीलयैव, 3.4).

The Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) also pictures the Goddess with eyes reddened by intoxication: name 432, मदघूर्णितरक्ताक्षी, ‘whose red eyes roll with intoxication’. The image is shared; the context there is not a battle.

A modern reading: the text puts the same word, मद, on the asura’s pride. The intoxication that matters in the story is his: he cannot see what he is fighting.

samasa.alt: It can also be read as a masculine accusative agreeing with तम्: Mahiṣa, ‘whose speech was confused by the flush of his face stirred up by pride (मद)’. The adverbial reading is preferred: it is the Goddess who has just drunk (3.34) and who speaks; the asura has only bellowed.

morph.note: Present participle of a curādi root (stem चूर्णय-) with the feminine suffix -ई: चूर्णयत् → चूर्णयन्ती. Her action runs while she speaks: ‘pulverising … she said’.
प्रहित ‘sent, hurled’ is the past participle of प्र + √हि ‘to send’; the identical-looking हित ‘placed’ belongs to √धा.
A neuter accusative singular can describe the manner of an action (kriyāviśeṣaṇa): ‘she spoke in such a way that …’. उद्धूत is the past participle of उद् + √धू ‘to shake up, stir’.

mantras.anvaya: सा च तेन प्रहितान् तान् शरोत्करैः चूर्णयन्ती मदोद्धूतमुखरागाकुलाक्षरं तम् उवाच।
mantras.anvaya_en: A present participle of accompanying action (चूर्णयन्ती) with its own object, then the main verb उवाच with its person addressed (तम्) and an adverbial compound of manner.
mantras.lit: And she, pulverising with volleys of arrows those (mountains) hurled by him, spoke to him in a manner in which (her) syllables were confused by the flush of (her) face stirred up by intoxication.
mantras.tr: Grinding to dust with volleys of arrows the mountains he hurled, she spoke to him, her face flushed with the drink and her words slurred:
mantras.tr_note: The long compound is taken as an adverb describing her speech; the alternative (describing the asura) is given in Samāsa.

comm.t: The verse introduces the Goddess’s only direct speech in the chapter (3.38). She speaks while still destroying his missiles: the words and the arrows come together. Readings differ over whose face is flushed: the compound fits the Goddess, who has just drunk, and can grammatically describe the asura instead (see Samāsa).

flags.uncertain: The reference of मदोद्धूतमुखरागाकुलाक्षरम् (the Goddess’s speech, adverbial; or the asura, agreeing with तम्) is an interpretive choice; the adverbial reading is preferred.

mantras.anvaya: (हे) मूढ, यावत् अहं मधु पिबामि, (तावत्) क्षणं गर्ज गर्ज। मया त्वयि हते (सति) अत्र एव देवताः आशु गर्जिष्यन्ति।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two sentences: an imperative with a time clause (यावत् … with the correlative तावत् understood), then a future with a locative absolute.
mantras.lit: Roar, roar for a moment, O fool, while I drink the wine. When you have been slain by me, the gods will soon roar right here.
mantras.tr: Roar, fool, roar on for a moment, while I drink this wine. When I have slain you, it is the gods who will be roaring here — and soon.
mantras.tr_note: The second ‘roar’ is the gods’ shout of triumph; ‘it is the gods who’ brings out the contrast the repeated verb makes.

comm.t: The Goddess’s only speech in the chapter, and a taunt. The same verb, √गर्ज्, carries both halves: his roaring lasts a moment (क्षणम्), the gods’ roaring will follow his death on this very spot (अत्रैव). She names the drink मधु; the narrator called it ‘the supreme drink’ (3.34).
The line is among the best known of the Devī Māhātmya in recitation, and it is often heard as the Goddess’s complete assurance: the outcome is already decided while she drinks.
A modern reading: arrogance is loud and brief. The verse gives it its moment — क्षणम् — and does not answer it in kind.

mantras.anvaya: एवम् उक्त्वा समुत्पत्य सा तं महासुरम् आरूढा (सती) पादेन कण्ठे आक्रम्य च शूलेन एनम् अताडयत्।
mantras.anvaya_en: A chain of absolutives (उक्त्वा, समुत्पत्य, आक्रम्य) and a participle (आरूढा) leading to one finite verb, अताडयत्. कण्ठे is taken with आक्रम्य (‘pressing on the neck with her foot’); it can also go with अताडयत् (‘struck him on the neck’).
mantras.lit: Having spoken thus, leaping up, she mounted that great asura, and pressing (him) down on the neck with (her) foot, struck him with (her) spear.
mantras.tr: With these words she leapt up and mounted the great demon; pressing her foot on his neck, she struck him with her spear.

comm.t: Words become action at once. The Goddess’s foot on the buffalo’s neck and her spear in his body make the image the text is known for — the form painted and sculpted as Mahiṣāsuramardinī. The शूल is the one Śiva drew from his own trident and gave her (शूलं शूलाद्विनिष्कृष्य ददौ तस्यै पिनाकधृक्, 2.20).

mantras.anvaya: ततः तया पदा आक्रान्तः सः अपि ततः निजमुखात् अर्धनिष्क्रान्तः एव आसीत्, देव्याः वीर्येण संवृतः (सन्)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first ततः is ‘then’, the second ‘from there’ (from the buffalo body), defined by निजमुखात्. देव्याः may also be read as देव्या (instrumental, ‘by the Goddess’) with संवृतः; the spelling देव्या वीर्येण fits both.
mantras.lit: Then he too, pinned by her foot, from there, from his own mouth, had only half come out, held fast by the power of the Goddess.
mantras.tr: Pinned beneath her foot, the asura began to come forth from the buffalo’s mouth in his own form, but got only halfway, held fast by the Goddess’s power.
mantras.tr_note: ‘In his own form’ and ‘the buffalo’s mouth’ interpret निजमुखात् ततः: he emerges from the mouth of the body he is in. ‘Began to’ renders the sense of एव ‘only (half)’.

comm.t: The last transformation fails. Pinned by her foot, the asura tries to leave the buffalo body through its mouth and is caught halfway, held by the Goddess’s power.
Many images of Mahiṣāsuramardinī show exactly this moment: the asura in human form half emerged from the body of the buffalo, the Goddess’s foot or lion upon him.

A modern reading: the asura is caught between the shape he has worn and the one he is trying to escape into. Every earlier escape worked by changing form; this one is stopped in the middle of the change.

mantras.tr: Still only half emerged, still fighting, the great demon was struck down by the Goddess, who cut off his head with her great sword.
mantras.tr_note: The Sanskrit is passive; the English keeps the passive for the asura and turns the absolutive into a relative clause for the Goddess.

comm.t: The death of Mahiṣa. He fights to the end (युध्यमानः), half out of the buffalo; the Goddess beheads him with the great sword. The head she was about to cut off in 3.30 falls now. Among her gifts in chapter 2 the sword came from Kāla (कालश्च दत्तवान् खड्गम्, 2.24).
A modern reading: the end comes not when the asura is strongest but in the middle of a change he cannot complete — still fighting, still half of what he was.

mantras.anvaya: सुराः दिव्यैः महर्षिभिः सह तां देवीं तुष्टुवुः। गन्धर्वपतयः जगुः, अप्सरोगणाः च ननृतुः।
mantras.anvaya_en: Three clauses, each with its own subject and perfect verb: the gods praise, the Gandharvas sing, the Apsarases dance.
mantras.lit: The gods, together with the heavenly great seers, praised that Goddess; the lords of the Gandharvas sang, and the troupes of Apsarases danced.
mantras.tr: The gods, with the heavenly great sages, sang the Goddess’s praise; the Gandharva lords sang and the Apsarases danced.

comm.t: The chapter closes in celebration: praise, song and dance. तुष्टुवुः ‘they praised’ is taken up in the next chapter, where the gods led by Indra sing their hymn to the Goddess (तां तुष्टुवुः, 4.2).
In the Gita Press pāṭha this is the last mantra of the third chapter and carries the closing bīja ॐ, which belongs to the recitation, not to the verse.
